data.user_prompt: How do I structure a website for the UK, Poland and Russian-speaking readers?

sections.text:
For the **UK, Poland, and Russian-speaking readers**, the cleanest approach is usually to create **separate language/region URLs** on one domain, use **localized content**, and add **hreflang** for each version.[9][3][1]

A practical structure would be:

- **English for the UK**: `example.com/en-gb/`
- **Polish**: `example.com/pl-pl/`
- **Russian**: `example.com/ru/`

This follows the common recommendation to use **unique URLs for each language version** and to keep a consistent structure across the site.[9][3][12]

### Recommended setup

| Market | Suggested URL | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| UK readers | `example.com/en-gb/` | Use **English + UK regional targeting** |
| Poland | `example.com/pl-pl/` | Use **Polish content** |
| Russian-speaking readers | `example.com/ru/` or `example.com/ru-xx/` | Use `ru` if the content is for Russian speakers generally; use a region code only if you are targeting a specific country |

Google says to use **different URLs** for different language versions and to annotate them with **hreflang**.[9] For regional targeting, hreflang can include a region code such as **`en-GB`**.[2][7]

### Why this is usually best

- **Subdirectories** are commonly recommended because they keep all authority on one domain and are simpler to manage.[1][3][6]
- **Different URLs per language** help search engines index the correct version and reduce confusion between audiences.[9][12]
- **Localized slugs, titles, and metadata** are part of good multilingual SEO, not just direct translation.[1][11]

### How to implement it

- Put each version on its **own unique URL**.[1][9]
- Add **self-referencing canonical tags** on each version.[1][3]
- Add **hreflang annotations** between all versions so Google can match users to the right page.[9][3]
- Use a **language switcher** that lets users choose versions manually.[9][16]
- Avoid automatic redirects based only on IP or browser language, because Google advises against automatically redirecting users away from a language version they requested or could choose themselves.[9]

### Hreflang example

```html
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-gb" href="https://example.com/en-gb/page/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="pl-pl" href="https://example.com/pl-pl/page/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="ru" href="https://example.com/ru/page/" />
<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/en-gb/page/" />
```

Google recommends `hreflang` for language versions and locale-specific URLs for targeting by page or site level.[9] In practice, the `ru` page should usually be a real Russian-language version, not just an English page with a Russian selector.[9][16]

### One important decision

If by “Russian-speaking readers” you mean **Russian speakers in multiple countries**, then **`/ru/`** is often enough. If you mean a **specific country market** such as Kazakhstan or another region, then use a **language-region pair** like `ru-kz` where appropriate.[2][7]

If you want, I can turn this into a **recommended site map and hreflang plan** for your exact pages.
